analysis.one_liner: Caps Senate campaign spending, bans party soft money and foreign donations, and gives a tax credit for small contributions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Rules Committee on the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set spending ceilings for Senate campaigns, with candidates who exceeded them paying a fee that went to their opponents. It would have banned national party committees from raising or spending 'soft money' — the unlimited, unregulated donations that big contributors gave to parties outside normal limits — and tightened the ban on foreign nationals giving to campaigns. It also would have created a tax credit of up to $100 ($200 for joint filers) for people who gave small amounts to congressional candidates, to encourage ordinary voters to participate in funding campaigns. The bill never left the Rules Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would face campaigns less dominated by unlimited special-interest money; small donors, who would get a federal tax credit of up to $100 for contributing to congressional candidates; and candidates who volunteer to accept spending limits, who would gain a financial penalty against rivals who outspend them.

how_it_helps.text: Bans national, state, and local party committees from soliciting or spending money outside the federal limits, closing the 'soft money' channel that let large donors give unlimited sums through the parties [S2][S3].
Forbids federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting or receiving funds not subject to federal limits, limiting how much time incumbents must spend chasing large checks [S2][S3].

Caps spending in Senate elections (for example, a general-election ceiling with a floor of $950,000 and a cap of $5.5 million, scaled to state population), and candidates who exceed the limit pay a fee equal to 50 percent of the excess, which goes to opponents who stayed within the limits [S3].

Limits a Senate candidate's spending of personal and immediate-family money to the lesser of $250,000 or 10 percent of the spending limit, reducing the advantage of personally wealthy candidates [S3].
Creates a tax credit of up to $100 ($200 on joint returns) for contributions to congressional candidates, lowering the cost for ordinary voters to take part in financing elections [S2][S3].

Strengthens the ban on contributions by foreign nationals and redefines 'independent expenditure' to cover broadcast ads naming a candidate in the final 60 days, whether or not they use explicit 'vote for' language [S3].

analysis.who_pays: National party committees and large donors who used unlimited soft-money gifts to influence elections; candidates who want to outspend the new limits (they would pay a fee to opponents); personally wealthy candidates spending more than $250,000 of their own money; and broadcast stations, which would have to sell political ads at the lowest unit rate in more circumstances.

drawbacks.text: The spending caps are uniform dollar figures scaled only to state population; critics of spending limits argue that ceilings favor incumbents, who enter races with name recognition and free media, and can make it harder for challengers to become known [S3].

The bill does not address independent groups' ability to spend money outside the party system, so it could push money away from accountable parties toward harder-to-trace channels; it attempts to police this by redefining 'independent expenditure,' a definition likely to be challenged in court [S2][S3].
The voluntary structure means candidates can decline the limits entirely and instead pay a 50 percent fee on excess spending, which wealthy campaigns could simply absorb as a cost of winning [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the largest known loophole in campaign money of the era — unlimited soft money to party committees — and adds a genuine counterweight in the small-donor tax credit and the penalty for exceeding spending limits. Its weaknesses are real: caps can disadvantage underfunded challengers, and its enforcement relies on the FEC and voluntary compliance. On balance it is a sincere reform attempt with ordinary voters as its main intended beneficiaries and large donors and party committees as its main losers.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Rules Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never acted, no cosponsors ever signed on, and the bill died there when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Dorgan introduced the Campaign Finance Reform Act of 1997 on January 21, 1997, the first month of the new Congress [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration on the day of introduction; no further action appears in the record [S5].
No senator joined as a cosponsor during the two-year Congress [S4].
The bill never received a committee hearing, a floor vote, or action in the House, and expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent senators and the national party committees are better off, because the soft-money channel they relied on for unlimited contributions stayed open and no spending limits took effect. Large donors who fund campaigns outside normal contribution limits also benefit, since the rules the bill would have changed never changed.

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Campaign Finance Reform Act of 1997 and delivered introductory remarks; the bill attracted no cosponsors [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee [S5].

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.role: U.S. Senator from Kentucky; leading Senate opponent of campaign finance limits
against.what_they_did: Led Senate Republican resistance to campaign finance reform legislation in the 105th Congress, including blocking reform bills that had majority support from ever reaching an up-or-down vote.

against.name: National party committees
against.role: Republican and Democratic national and congressional campaign committees
against.what_they_did: Raised and spent large sums of unlimited soft money during the 1996 and 1998 cycles and resisted proposals to ban the practice.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill, so the record shows no roll-call split; its sole sponsor was a Democrat, it drew no cosponsors from either party, and campaign finance fights in this Congress generally split along party lines over soft money.

industries.note: Soft money was their main source of unlimited funding; the ban would have ended that revenue stream, which they used to fund ads and party activity that influence federal elections. Their gain from the bill's failure is ordinary voters' loss of a rule that would have limited the influence of large gifts.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and special-interest givers
industries.note: The bill would have blocked federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting funds outside federal limits and capped candidate spending, reducing the leverage of big checks. Its failure preserved the existing system of large-donor access.

The bill would extend the lowest-unit-rate requirement to candidate-image ads and tighten the definition of electioneering broadcasts, cutting the premium rates stations charge during campaigns. Political advertising is profitable for broadcasters, so their interest runs against cheaper, better-regulated campaign airtime.
